title: The Ledger
sample: A sample book. Raymond and his family are fictional. The voice is synthetic.

memories.title: My father’s caliper
memories.body:
My father fixed cars on South Flores Street. Six kids, one bay, and a sign he painted himself. Ortiz Auto. No first name on it, because he said the name was the family’s, not his.

I was the fourth boy. The three older ones got the wrenches. I got the broom, and then the parts washer, and then, when I was eleven, the caliper. Six-inch dial, Brown and Sharpe. He’d bought it used from a man who was closing a machine shop on the east side, and it cost him more than he’d admit to my mother.

He put it in my hand and said, this one measures. The rest of the tools in here guess.

Every job in that bay ended the same way. You wiped down the engine, you wiped down the fender where your arm had been, you put the tools back in the order they came out. Leave the engine cleaner than you found it. He said it in Spanish and in English, depending on who was listening. I heard it ten thousand times before I was fifteen.

I didn’t understand it until I had my own floor. It isn’t about clean. It’s about the next man. The customer opens the hood and sees that somebody cared. The next mechanic finds the tools where they belong. You’re not finishing a job. You’re handing it to someone.

The caliper is on my desk. It reads a thousandth heavy. I’ve known that since 1962 and I’ve never had it fixed, because then I’d have to learn it over again. When I measure something that matters, I use it anyway, and I take the thousandth off in my head. That’s what he left me. A tool that’s a little wrong and the knowledge of which way.

memories.title: A broom on Roosevelt Avenue
memories.body:
I was supposed to finish high school. I finished most of it. In the spring of 1968 a man named Walt Brenner came into my father’s bay with a Pontiac that wouldn’t idle, and while my father fixed it he watched me deburr a bracket with a file. He had a job shop on Roosevelt Avenue, eleven men, and he needed a kid to sweep. A dollar sixty an hour. I still have the first stub.

I swept for four months. Then the second-shift lathe man quit on a Friday and Walt said, you’ve been watching, get on it. I turned bushings until two in the morning and scrapped nine of the first twenty. He didn’t fire me. He showed me where my hand was wrong.

That’s the whole trade, if you want it in one line. Somebody shows you where your hand is wrong and you don’t make them show you twice.

I stayed six years. By 1974 I could set up anything in the building and Walt was paying me three dollars and a quarter, which was the most he could pay anybody. A supplier’s rep told me the furniture plants in Michigan were hiring tool and die men and couldn’t find enough. I’d never been north of Dallas. I had two hundred and sixty dollars and a 1966 Ford Falcon.

I drove to Grand Rapids in October without a job waiting. Sight unseen. My mother cried at the curb and my father handed me the caliper, in its case, and said, don’t lose it. For keeps this time. He never said don’t go. I think he knew there was nothing on South Flores Street for a fourth son but the broom.

I got hired the second day. Tool and die, southwest side, four dollars and ten cents. I called home from a pay phone and my mother asked if it was cold. It was. I said no.

memories.title: The window at the credit union
memories.body:
My first Michigan paycheck was for sixty-one hours. I didn’t have a bank. The foreman said go to the credit union on Division, they’ll take anybody.

There were three windows and two were open. I picked the one with the girl who wasn’t smiling. That was Elena. She looked at my deposit slip, looked at me, and said, you added this wrong. I had. By four dollars, in my favor. She fixed it with a pencil and didn’t say anything else, and I stood there like a man who’d forgotten what he came in for.

I went back every Friday for eleven weeks. I never needed to. You could mail a deposit. She knew that and I knew that and neither of us brought it up.

The twelfth Friday she handed my receipt back with something written on it. Her mother’s phone number, and the words Sunday, two o’clock, bring nothing. Her mother did not trust a man who showed up with flowers. I showed up with nothing and ate three plates.

We were married in August 1975 at her mother’s parish. Her father told me at the reception, in Spanish, that she had never once been wrong about money, and I’d do well to remember it. I thought it was a toast. It was instructions.

Marisol came in 1977 and Tomás in 1980. Elena kept the books for a dry cleaner and a plumber from the kitchen table, for cash, so she could stay home. I didn’t know I was watching the best bookkeeper in Kent County learn her trade.

memories.title: Spring Lake, the first week of August
memories.body:
Elena made one rule when we started the shop. The first week of August, the doors close, everybody paid, nobody in the building. Especially me. Once we could afford it, every August we rented the same cottage on Spring Lake.

I couldn’t swim. Where I grew up the pool on our side of town was closed more than it was open, and then I was working. I’d stand in the lake up to my knees and call it swimming.

Then Tomás learned at the Y. He was seven. He walked out to where I was standing and said, Dad, put your face in. It’s just water. I said I knew it was just water. He said, then put your face in.

It took three Augusts. He never laughed and he counted out loud. That’s how I taught him the lathe when he was sixteen.

I can swim the length of a dock now. Elena says that’s plenty.

sides.name: Marisol Ortiz, his daughter
sides.body: He says three Augusts. It was four. The last one he swam in front of Mom on purpose. She clapped from her chair like it was the Olympics. He walked very slowly to his towel.

memories.title: A garage on Godfrey Avenue
memories.body:
I had a good job. I was the best setup man at a tool and die shop on the southwest side, and I knew it, and so did they. What I couldn’t stand was watching parts go out late because nobody upstairs would listen to the floor. We’d tell them the fixture was wrong on Monday and they’d find out it was wrong on Thursday, and it was our fault on Friday.

In August 1983 I rented a two-car garage on Godfrey Avenue for $180 a month and bought a used Bridgeport mill for $2,300. Elena’s savings were $6,000. The credit union gave us $5,000 more, because she’d worked there and they remembered her. That was the whole company. Eleven thousand dollars and a mill.

That first winter I worked in my coat. The only heat was a kerosene heater and the machine. The mill was the only thing in there making money, so it got the heat first. I’d stand close to it between cuts.

Elena came at noon with lunch in a coffee can and sat on an upturned bucket while I ate. She brought the ledger. She always brought the ledger. On Saturdays Marisol drew on the floor in chalk, and Tomás slept in a parts box lined with a moving blanket.

The first order was $412. Twelve brackets for a chair company. I still have the first one, in a frame, and how it got there is a story for later.

memories.title: Elena’s ledger
memories.body:
Your grandmother was the most important person in that company, and nobody knew it. That’s not even a question.

For twenty-one years, most nights after the kids were down and all day Sunday, she sat at this table with a green ledger, a pencil and an adding machine. Everything with a dollar sign. She chased the late invoices. She handled the bank. She told me which jobs were losing money, usually before I wanted to hear it, and she was never wrong, which was worse.

She was never on the payroll. She wasn’t on the incorporation papers. Customers who called the house thought she was the receptionist. She let them.

In 1991, when we nearly went under, it was her ledger that showed the bank a way through. Not my machines. Her pencil.

She went on the papers as a partner in 2004. Twenty-one years late. I was proud and I was stupid, and in 1983 those were the same thing. I thought the company was the machines. It was the machines and the money, and she ran the money.

sides.name: Marisol Ortiz, his daughter
sides.body: I was eight. Mom had a column that wouldn’t foot and she’d been at it an hour. I was doing homework across from her and I said, Mom, the seven’s a one. It was. She didn’t say good girl. She slid the ledger over and said, check the rest. I checked the rest. That’s the night I got my job, whatever my business card says now.

memories.title: Hiring Hector
memories.body:
By spring of ’84 I had more work than hands. I put a card on the board at the hardware store on Division. Machinist wanted, must own tools. Three men called. Two wanted to know the pay first.

Hector Ruiz asked what I was making. Brackets, I said. He asked what tolerance. I told him, and he said, on a Bridgeport? And I said yes, and he said, all right, I’ll come look.

He came and looked. He walked over to the mill and ran his thumb along the table, the way you check for chips, and then he wiped the table with his rag. I hired him before he’d said what he wanted an hour. It was $7.50. He stayed thirty-eight years. I never put another card on that board.

memories.title: My father comes north
memories.body:
My father came north once. June 1985, on the Greyhound, because he didn’t trust airplanes or my driving.

I wanted him to see the garage on Godfrey Avenue, the mill, the work on the board, the sign. He walked around it a long time and didn’t say anything.

Then he found Elena’s mother’s fan on my bench and fixed it. He couldn’t be in a room with tools and not work. When he was done he wiped the bench where his arm had been.

Outside he looked at the sign. Ortiz Precision. He said, no first name. Good.

He died in March 1987. Elena took the call on the hall phone. We drove to San Antonio in twenty-two hours.

I didn’t cry at the funeral. I cried at a gas station in Texarkana on the way home.

He only came north once. I spent it showing him the mill. I should have shown him the kids.

memories.title: The customer who was sixty percent
memories.body:
The most expensive mistake I ever made came in on a Tuesday in 1986, and it looked like the best day of my life.

Twelve thousand brackets a month for a big office-furniture maker on the lakeshore. One purchase order. I hired four people that week and bought a second mill on credit. By 1988 we were twelve people in a real building. By 1990 that one customer was sixty percent of everything Ortiz Precision made.

It felt like winning. It was a trap with a nice paint job.

In January 1991 their purchasing manager called to say volumes were being cut in half, effective immediately. No warning. No appeal. He was sorry, and he was reading it off a sheet. I put the phone down and went out on the floor and ran a part myself. I didn’t trust myself to talk to anybody.

After that Elena drew a line in pencil across the front page of every ledger. One customer, no more than a quarter of us. We turned down work to stay under that line, good work, more than once. Tomás runs his own shop by it now. He calls it Dad’s quarter. It should be called Mom’s.

memories.title: The Friday I couldn’t make payroll
memories.body:
It was February 8, 1991, a Friday, two weeks after the call from the lakeshore. Fourteen people, and the money for payroll wasn’t there. I’d done the arithmetic four times and it came out the same four times.

I sat in the truck in the parking lot for an hour. I didn’t go in. Elena came out at nine with the green ledger under her arm, got in the passenger side, and opened it on the dash. She said, there’s enough for everyone if we don’t pay us. Four months, maybe five, if the furniture people don’t cut again.

So we didn’t pay us. Four months. We ate what was in the freezer and she never once mentioned it at the table.

Then I had to tell the fourteen.

I stood on a pallet at the back of the floor at three o’clock and told them the truth. We’d lost a third of our work and I didn’t know if we’d make it. Payroll was covered through June because Elena and I were taking nothing. After that I couldn’t promise. Two men quit that afternoon, and I didn’t blame them. Twelve stayed.

They stayed because I told them first. Before the bank, before the customer. People can take bad news. What they can’t take is finding out last.

Five of the twelve were still there in 2022, and they own part of it now. Every one of them got paid that Friday by noon, and every Friday after, and I’d stand on that pallet again tomorrow.

memories.title: Who gets the keys
memories.body:
Nobody in this family talks about 2019, so I’ll go first.

Tomás wanted to run the company. He’d been on the floor since he was sixteen and in the office since 2008, and he was ready. I said not yet. I said it in 2014 and I said it in 2016 and I’m told I said it a few more times after that.

The honest reason is I didn’t know what the company was without me in it. I’d walked that floor every morning for thirty-six years. If I handed Tomás the keys, I was going to be a man who used to own a machine shop, and I couldn’t see him yet.

In March 2019 a private equity firm put an offer on my desk. An outfit that buys companies with borrowed money and sells the pieces. They’d move half the work to Mexico. I kept it on my desk three months and didn’t tell Tomás. That was wrong.

Hector found out. He asked who was going to tell the ones who stayed in 1991. I didn’t have an answer, so that was the answer.

It was Elena’s idea and Tomás did the work. Fine. Both. The keys went to the people on the floor. Tomás got his own shop, and Hector.

sides.name: Tomás Ortiz, his son
sides.body: You said not yet for five years, Dad. Not a few times. Five years, and I counted. I’d have taken the keys in 2016 and I’d have been fine. What I’ll give him is this: when that offer came, he was more scared of it than I was. That’s when I knew he wasn’t keeping the company from me. He was keeping it from them. After the sale I opened my own shop. He didn’t argue. He sent Hector.

sides.name: Elena Ortiz, his wife
sides.body: I read an article about a company in Ohio that sold itself to the people who worked there. I cut it out and put it on his desk, under the offer, and I left it there a month. I moved it to the top every Monday until he read it.

memories.title: Selling it to the people who built it
memories.body:
The private equity offer was the better deal on paper. I’m not going to pretend otherwise.

In the end I took about a fifth less and sold the company to the people who worked there. An employee stock ownership plan. A piece of it for every one of them. The better part of three years and four lawyers to build, and I understood maybe half of what the lawyers said, and Marisol understood the other half and translated. A hundred and forty people. Every one of them in Grand Rapids.

My last day was a Friday in March 2022. Payday. I signed the payroll one more time, by hand, the way I had since 1983, and then I walked the floor.

At the end of first shift they called me to the back. Hector had something under a towel. A frame, and in the frame the first bracket I ever made in the garage on Godfrey Avenue. He’d kept it in his toolbox for thirty-eight years. I didn’t know. I’d thought it was gone.

It runs without me, which was the whole idea.

sides.name: Hector Ruiz, his first employee
sides.body: He gave me that bracket my first morning, in 1984. Said, match this. I matched it. Then I put his in the bottom of my box under the parallels, because I figured a man who starts a company in a garage is going to want the first part back someday and won’t think to keep it himself. I was right. Thirty-eight years. He cried. He’ll say he didn’t.

memories.title: Thursdays
memories.body:
I go in on Thursdays. Nobody asked me to and nobody’s told me to stop. I walk the floor before anybody’s read their email, the way I always did, and I say good morning to a hundred and forty people and I don’t know all their names anymore. Then I stand by the Bridgeport for a while. It’s at the front of the shop. Every new hire makes a first part on it. Forty-two years and it still holds a thousandth.

Nobody needs me there. Best feeling I’ve had in forty years. I’m home by eleven and Elena asks how it was and I say, running.

Last spring Maya brought a drawing to the shop. Her own company, her own part. A housing for a circuit board, aluminum, and she needed one to show people before she could pay anybody to make a thousand. She asked if she could use the Bridgeport.

I said I’d run it. She said no, Grandpa, I’ll run it, you watch. So I watched. She’d never run a manual mill in her life. She scrapped the first one. On the second one she stopped a thousandth short and checked it and looked at me, and I said, that’s my father’s caliper talking. She’d taken it off my desk that morning without asking. I didn’t say anything about that. He wouldn’t have either.

The part came out right. I don’t understand what goes inside it. She’s explained it four times. I’m going to get it on the fifth.

sides.name: Maya Ortiz, his granddaughter
sides.body: I went with him one Thursday in October. The first-shift lead had a list on a clipboard. Four questions, saved up all week, and she waited until he’d done his walk before she asked them. He answered all four in under a minute each and said, you didn’t need me for that. She said, no, Ray. Then she wrote the answers down.
